notes.meaning: Cornelius was an army captain stationed in Caesarea, the center of Roman government in Judea. He commanded about a hundred soldiers in a unit made up of men from Italy. God chose this Gentile soldier to be the first uncircumcised outsider welcomed into the Christian church.

Cornelius turned away from Roman idols to worship the one true God, and he taught his entire household to do the same. He showed his faith by praying regularly and giving money generously to poor Jewish people. Even in the rough life of a military commander, his faith produced true kindness and devotion.

Around three o'clock in the afternoon, during the usual Jewish time of prayer, Cornelius was praying in his home. While fully awake, he saw an angel of God arrive in a clear vision. The angel called him by his own name, showing that God knew him and cared about him personally.

Cornelius stared at the angel in fear and asked what God wanted with him. The angel told him that his prayers and his gifts to the poor had risen up to heaven like a pleasing sacrifice that God remembered. God was now stepping in to give him greater light and understanding.

differ.view: Cornelius was already born again by the Holy Spirit and had saving faith like Old Testament believers, which is why God accepted his prayers.
Cornelius did not yet have saving faith in Christ, but God graciously accepted his sincere seeking through prayer and charity.

notes.meaning: The angel commanded Cornelius to send men down the coast to the port city of Joppa to fetch Simon Peter. Peter was staying by the sea at the home of another Simon, who worked as a leather tanner. God used an angel to start the connection, but He chose a human preacher to share the message of Jesus.

As soon as the angel left, Cornelius obeyed without any delay. He summoned two trusted servants and a God-fearing soldier from his staff, explained the entire vision to them, and sent them toward Joppa. His quick obedience showed his deep hunger to know whatever God had in store for him.

Around noon the next day, as the messengers were nearing Joppa, Peter climbed up onto the flat roof of the house to pray. Roofs in that region were private, quiet places where people could get away from daily chores to seek God. While the visitors were walking toward the gate, God was already preparing Peter's heart to receive them.

Peter became very hungry while waiting for the midday meal to be cooked. While he was praying, God brought him into a trance, lifting his mind above ordinary earthly thoughts so he could receive direct revelation. God used Peter's physical hunger as the setting for an important spiritual lesson.

Peter saw the sky open and something like a huge linen sheet let down to the earth by its four corners. Inside were all sorts of four-legged animals, reptiles, and birds, mixing creatures the Jewish law allowed with those it called unclean. This unusual sight caught Peter's full attention and set up a startling test of his faith.

A heavenly voice commanded Peter to get up, slaughter the creatures, and eat them. This challenged everything Peter had practiced since childhood, because God's law through Moses strictly forbade eating unclean animals. The command invited Peter to step past an ancient boundary that had long kept Jews separate from all other nations.

Peter replied with a polite but firm refusal, telling the Lord that he had never once in his life eaten anything unholy or unclean. Even though he recognized the voice of his Master, he clung to the written food laws he had carefully kept since childhood. He could not yet see why God would ask him to break rules he had always honored.

The voice spoke again, warning Peter not to call unholy what God Himself had cleansed. God had put the Old Testament food laws in place for a season, but He was now setting them aside. While the words spoke about animals, their real point was that Gentile people were no longer to be kept away as unclean.

This exchange happened three times so that Peter would have no lingering doubts about what God was saying. Then the sheet was pulled back up into heaven, proving that this message came straight from God. Repeating the lesson made sure that this life-changing truth would stick in Peter's mind.

Peter came out of the trance completely puzzled about what the vision meant, but right then the men sent by Cornelius arrived at the outside gate. They called out to ask if Simon Peter was staying there. God guided the timing so that real events at the door would explain the mystery of the vision.

While Peter was still turning the vision over in his mind, the Holy Spirit told him that three men were looking for him downstairs. The Spirit commanded him to go down and travel with them without second-guessing or holding back, because God Himself had sent them. Peter was called to obey the Spirit's voice even before he knew the travelers' names or their errand.

Peter went down to the entrance and told the men that he was the person they were seeking. He asked them plainly why they had traveled all the way to find him. His ready greeting showed that he was willing to follow God's direction step by step, even while still learning what it all meant.

The messengers explained that Cornelius was a Roman commander who lived uprightly, revered God, and had the respect of the local Jewish community. They reported that a holy angel had instructed him to bring Peter to his house so he could listen to God's message. Their report assured Peter that God was already doing a special work in this Gentile home.

Peter set aside strict Jewish traditions by inviting these Gentile guests inside to stay for the night. The following morning he set out with them, taking six Jewish believers from Joppa along to serve as witnesses. Peter's warm welcome showed that his vision had already begun breaking down his old prejudices.

The travelers arrived in Caesarea the next day, where Cornelius was eagerly waiting for them. Cornelius had gathered his relatives and close friends so that they could hear Peter's message too. His loving invitation showed that he did not want to keep God's truth to himself, but wanted everyone he cared about to share in it.
